content.title: About
content.content: Beef taco filling is a ready‑to‑heat mixture of ground beef, cheese, tomato and a specially seasoned taco sauce. It is designed for quick preparation of Mexican dishes such as tacos, burritos and fajitas.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional Mexican taco filling is cooked on a skillet with chili, cumin and paprika spices.
The cheese blend often combines cheddar and mozzarella for optimal meltability.
Tomatoes give the filling a fresh, slightly tangy flavor and a vibrant color.
Taco sauce typically contains vinegar, sugar and aromatic spices, creating a sweet‑spicy balance.
The beef is usually browned until a golden crust forms, locking in juiciness.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Beef provides a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Beef supplies easily absorbable heme iron, supporting healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese adds calcium, important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both beef and cheese are good sources of B12, B6 and niacin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Lycopene from tomatoes
items.content: Tomatoes contain lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Beef and cheese can be high in saturated fats; people with elevated cholesterol should watch portion sizes.

items.title: Salt in the sauce
items.content: Taco sauce often contains a notable amount of sodium, so choose a reduced‑salt version if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improper storage of the ready‑made filling can lead to bacterial growth; keep it refrigerated and observe use‑by dates.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the filling in a skillet or microwave, then spoon it into soft or crunchy taco shells. Top with fresh vegetables, guacamole, sour cream or salsa as desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days. For longer keeping, freeze in an airtight container for up to 2 months. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Butter is a dairy product made by churning cream. It is mostly milk fat (usually at least 80%), water, and a small amount of milk proteins. It has a delicate creamy flavor. Butter is used on sandwiches, in porridge, with vegetables, in baking, in sauces, and for frying. It comes salted and unsalted, as well as clarified (ghee).

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: When cream is churned, the milk fat gathers into butter, and the liquid part remains as buttermilk.
Butter's yellow shade depends on the animals' feed and its beta-carotene content.
Clarified butter (ghee) is free of water and milk proteins, so it tolerates high heat better.
It takes about 20 liters of milk to make one kilogram of butter.
Butter melts at a temperature close to body temperature, which is why it melts so smoothly in the mouth.

items.title: Contains vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A is fat-soluble and important for vision and skin.

items.title: Contains other fat-soluble vitamins
items.content: Butter provides small amounts of vitamins D, E, and K.

items.title: Contains butyrate
items.content: Butyric acid (butyrate) is a short-chain fatty acid naturally present in milk fat.

items.title: Source of energy
items.content: Butter provides a lot of energy, which is useful when energy needs are high.

items.title: Rich flavor
items.content: Because butter tastes so rich, a small amount is enough to flavor dishes.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Butter is rich in saturated fat, and too much can raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Butter is very high in calories, so portions should be moderate.

items.title: Milk components
items.content: Butter contains traces of lactose and milk proteins, so people with a milk allergy should avoid it.

items.title: Salt and burning
items.content: Salted butter can add to salt intake, and at high heat butter burns and smokes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spread butter on bread, add it to porridge, vegetables, mashed potatoes, and sauces, or use it in baking. For frying, use medium heat so the milk proteins do not burn, or choose clarified butter (ghee). A small amount is enough for flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store butter in the refrigerator in its original wrapper or in a covered butter dish, away from strong-smelling foods. The piece you are using can be kept at room temperature for one to two days in a cool place. For long-term storage, freeze butter, where it keeps for several months. Discard butter that smells rancid, has mold, or has changed color.

content.title: About
content.content: Tuna is a group of large, fast-swimming saltwater fish from the genus Thunnus and related species, including yellowfin, bluefin, albacore, bigeye, and skipjack. It has firm, meaty flesh that ranges from pink to deep red. Tuna is eaten fresh as steaks and sashimi, and is also widely sold canned or pouched.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tuna are among the fastest fish in the sea and swim long distances across oceans.
Some tuna species can partly regulate their body temperature, which is unusual among fish.
Canned light tuna is often skipjack, while canned white tuna is albacore.
Bluefin tuna is highly prized for sushi and sashimi, especially in Japan.
Canned tuna is sold packed in water, oil, or sauce.

items.title: Lean source of protein
items.content: Tuna provides high-quality protein with relatively little fat.

items.title: Contains omega-3 fatty acids
items.content: Tuna provides EPA and DHA, with higher amounts in fattier types such as bluefin and albacore.

items.title: Provides vitamin D and B vitamins
items.content: Tuna contains vitamin D, vitamin B12, niacin, and vitamin B6.

items.title: Rich in selenium
items.content: Selenium supports thyroid function and antioxidant defenses.

items.title: Convenient and long-lasting
items.content: Canned tuna is a shelf-stable source of protein.

items.title: Mercury
items.content: Tuna can contain mercury, with higher levels in larger species such as bigeye, bluefin, and albacore. Pregnant women and young children should follow local guidance on which tuna to eat and how often.

items.title: Histamine poisoning
items.content: Tuna that has been stored at improper temperatures can cause scombroid poisoning, so keep it cold.

items.title: Raw fish
items.content: Raw tuna can carry bacteria and parasites and is not recommended for pregnant women, young children, or people with weakened immunity.

items.title: Allergic reactions and sodium
items.content: Fish allergy can be serious, and canned tuna may contain added salt.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fresh tuna can be grilled, seared, baked, or eaten as sashimi or poke from a reliable source. Canned tuna can be used in salads, sandwiches, pasta, casseroles, and patties. Choose tuna packed in water or in olive oil according to your preference.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh tuna in the refrigerator and cook it within one to two days, or freeze it for longer storage. Unopened canned tuna keeps for a long time in a cool, dry place. Once opened, transfer canned tuna to an airtight container, refrigerate it, and eat it within three to four days.
